newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: PLO to lobby at U.N against Israeli building plan.
newsitem.headline: PLO to lobby at U.N against Israeli building plan.

text.p: The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) said on Wednesday it intended to lobby U.N. members to try to block a controversial Israeli building plan in an area southeast of Jerusalem.
"Many Israeli officials are indicating their intention of building a new settlement in East Jerusalem in the area of Jabal Abu Ghneim," the PLO's U.N. observer, Nasser al-Kidwa, said.
He was referring to a plan to construct 6,500 homes on a hill of pine trees between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, called Har Homa by Israel.

Addressing the first meeting this year of the 23-member U.N. committee on the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, al-Kidwa said the Security Council considered the same issue in May 1995 but had been unable to act because of a veto.

The United States then blocked a resolution that would have called on Israel to rescind the expropriation of 131 acres (53 hectares) of land in areas of Jerusalem captured in the 1967 Middle East war.
"Now we are having the same issue, hinging on the whole peace process, and probably threatening its integrity," al-Kidwa said.

"We will start some contacts in this regard here at the United Nations with the aim of avoiding the very serious harm which could be inflicted on the peace process. The aim, of course, is to guarantee that the Israeli plan is not going to be implemented, that no decision will be taken in this regard next week."
A spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in Jerusalem a decision on a date for building would be made at a ministerial meeting next week.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said during a visit to Ankara on Wednesday that the "settlement is completely illegal and it is against the U.N. conclusions and the agreements which we signed."
Al-Kidwa said he would hold consultations with various U.N. groups, especially the Arab group, and hoped the Palestine rights committee would help.
"Avoiding such serious problems is definitely essential for the continuation of the peace process," he said.

He noted that Arafat would visit U.S. President Bill Clinton in Washington on March 3, following a White House visit last week by Netanyahu and in advance of similar trips by President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt and King Hussein of Jordan.

"We do hope that all these visits will lead to some tangible improvements in the overall situation. But we remain reliant on international legitimacy, on the United Nations, the Security Council and on this committee," al-Kidwa said.
